columns.means: the currency's code. Five are used across the sales: USD, EUR, GBP, CAD, AUD.

concepts.means: The money a sale is denominated in: five ISO codes, pointed at by every sale and by both ends of every exchange rate. The account is ontology/concepts/Currency.md.

columns.means: the row key: one row per customer. The register is not the buyer list — many customers have never ordered (rule Customer.register_not_buyers).
the customer's name as registered.
the continent the customer lives on.
the country the CUSTOMER lives in. No customer carries the `--` online placeholder. This is the only column that can place an internet sale in a real country.
the state, province or region the customer lives in.
the city the customer lives in.
the customer's recorded gender.
the customer's date of birth.

the day this customer record became valid — the start of the validity window that says whether a customer is active on a reference date. The register is kept as a history, so a sale could in principle be attributed to where the customer lived ON THE ORDER DATE — nothing in this bundle declares that it should be.
the day this customer record stopped being valid — the last day of the validity window, as the source states it. Paired with `valid_from`.

the day after `valid_to`: the half-open end of the validity window, made by the transform. A record is valid on a day when `valid_from` is on or before it and `valid_end` is after it, which selects exactly the records `valid_to` on or after that day selects. It is what rule Customer.active_on_the_reference_date reads; offered to no question on its own.

concepts.means: A person on Contoso's customer register, each with a name, a birth date and a place — continent, country, state, city. The register is not the buyer list: many registered customers have never ordered (rule Customer.register_not_buyers). The account is ontology/concepts/Customer.md.

columns.means: the day the rate held.
the currency being converted FROM. Every currency appears as a source, so the view is a full matrix of currency pairs and not a USD-only lookup.
the currency being converted TO.

what one unit of `from_currency` was worth in `to_currency` on `date_day`. Same-currency pairs are present and are exactly 1. THE AMOUNTS ON A SALES LINE ARE ALREADY USD, so converting them with this is how a figure silently becomes the wrong currency. ITS AVERAGE IS THE PLAIN MEAN OF THE DAILY RATES, disclosed — one rate per day and ordered pair, the European Central Bank euro reference rate crossed through EUR, a day without a quote carrying the last quoted day's rate, and no traded volume behind any rate to weight it by (evidence in ontology/concepts/ExchangeRate.md, "How the rate averages"). An amount is still converted at its own day's rate, never at an averaged one (rule ExchangeRate.convert_per_day).

concepts.means: What one currency was worth in another on one day: a quoted rate over a date and an ordered pair of currencies. The account is ontology/concepts/ExchangeRate.md.

columns.means: THE SITE ITSELF — one row per site, which is what makes this relation the place a question about sites should be answered from. The value -1 is the online placeholder and not a place (rule Location.channel). City exists only on the CUSTOMER (`dim_customer.city`), where it is declared personally identifying (`offers.suppressed: DQ-IDENTIFYING-DIM_CUSTOMER-CITY`) and says where a customer lives, not where a shop stands. Surfacing `city` here would bind "which cities" to an INTEGER site code and present codes as city names; unbound, the question fails to bind and the walk says so, which is the correct outcome for a fact this bundle does not hold.
the country the site sits in.
the name of the country the site sits in, carried here as well as on dim_country.
the state, province or region the site sits in.
how many store rows have ever stood at this site. A site re-tenanted has several store rows over time; each is one premises (rule Store.premises_not_place).

true on the online placeholder (site code -1, which is not a place), false on every physical site, never empty. Made by the transform so that rule Location.channel reads `physical` as false and `online` as true instead of a stored value; it selects exactly the rows the code test selected. Offered to no question on its own: a question reaches it through the rule.
true where a store at this site has closed (at least one of its store rows carries a closing date), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Location.closed reads its `ever` option from it.
true where no store at this site trades (every one of its store rows carries a closing date), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Location.closed reads its `now` option from it.

concepts.means:
THE PLACE a store stands on — a country and a state, and nothing that belongs to the shop itself. Floor area, opening and closing dates are properties of PREMISES and live on Store; what a place owns is where it is.
ONE PLACE MAY HOLD A SUCCESSION OF PREMISES over time, which is the fact this concept exists to keep separate from Store: `dim_store.store_key` declares `finer_than: location_code`, so premises roll UP into a place and a place never divides down into one. Summing a per-premises measure over a place that has been re-let counts it once per tenancy.
A PLACE IS NOT A CITY IN THIS BUNDLE. Its finest geography is `state`, which in France means regions and overseas territories; `main.store` carries no city or town column. City exists only on the customer, as where a customer lives, and is declared personally identifying.
No counts here, by the ruling of 2026-10-24 — they belong in data/profiles/dim_location.yaml where they can be re-measured. The account is ontology/concepts/Location.md.

columns.means: the order this line belongs to; with `line_number` it is this relation's key. An order has one or more lines. The order header is a degenerate dimension here, not a second fact (rule Order.is_the_purchase).
which line of the order this is, 0 to 6. One order can hold several products, and the line is the grain of this fact.
the day the order was placed. THE PERIOD COLUMN: an unqualified question about when is answered on this and not on `delivery_date` (Order.date).
the day the order was delivered. Measured: never before `order_date` and never null. NOT the period a question is answered on unless it says delivery.
the customer who bought, joining dim_customer. The only route from a sale to a PERSON, and so the only way to attribute internet sales to a country.

the store the sale was rung up at, joining dim_store. Store key `999999` is the single online outlet, and `channel` beside this column states that split on the fact itself — so a question no longer has to reach dim_store to learn which channel a sale was in.

true on every web-shop line, false on every shop line, never empty; the same split as `channel`, as true / false. Made by the transform so that rule Order.channel reads its `shops` and `online` options from a column instead of a stored value.
the product sold, joining dim_product.

THE CURRENCY THE SALE WAS TRANSACTED IN, and NOT the unit of the amounts on this row. The amounts are USD. Filtering on this and presenting the amounts as if they were in that currency is forbidden by currency.ambiguity.code_is_not_the_unit_of_the_amounts.
how many units of the product the line sold.

what the customer was actually charged for the line, in USD, after discount: exactly `quantity * net_price`. THE DEFAULT MONEY COLUMN: a question saying revenue or sales without saying net or gross is answered here (rule Order.revenue_means_net). AN UNQUALIFIED PRICE means what the customer paid per article: this column summed and divided by `quantity` summed (operator ruling, 2026-09-30; rule Order.price_is_per_article). When a question says store, shop, product, or placed without naming a competing figure, those words are read on this same sales-line figure.
what the line would have cost at list price, in USD: exactly `quantity * unit_price`, on every line. The figure BEFORE discount.
what the goods on the line cost Contoso, in USD. Measured: exactly `quantity * unit_cost`.
the money given away on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `gross_amount - net_amount`. Upstream the discount is an integer percent from a closed set of 15 steps, 0 to 14.
the profit on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `net_amount - cost_amount`, so it is margin on the DISCOUNTED price and not on list.

what ONE UNIT ON THIS LINE was charged before discount, in USD. Measured against the source: `unit_price = product.Price × f`, where `f` is the same per-line factor used for `unit_cost = product.Cost × f`. From 2024 onward `f = 1.0`, so this is the current list price level for all products sold in that period. `gross_amount` is exactly `quantity * unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: Σ(quantity × unit_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `gross_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line prices (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").

the price actually paid for one unit, in USD, after discount. Upstream: `unit_price * (1 - discount/100)`, and measured never above `unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: the price holds for every unit on the line, so it averages as Σ(quantity × net_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `net_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_is_per_article), never as a plain mean of line prices. The generator draws a quantity per order row and prices the row per unit (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").

what one unit cost Contoso, in USD. Upstream it is scaled by the same price factor as `unit_price`, so margin PERCENT is stable within a category while absolute margin moves — a margin-erosion story read off this data is an artefact of the generator. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`; Σ(quantity × unit_cost) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `cost_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line costs (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").

concepts.means: One customer's purchase on one date, counted by distinct `order_key` over the line relation. It is also THE FACT NODE of the sales line, one row per order line - every money and quantity measure (net, gross, cost, discount, margin, units, and the per-unit prices) is a column it serves, and every edge from the sale to a dimension starts here. The account is ontology/concepts/Order.md.

columns.means:

A shop has its own name, floor area, opening date and closing date, because those are properties of premises and not of a place. `999999` is the online outlet.

the state, province or region the store sits in, within its country.
the day the store opened for trade.
the day the store closed, or null if it is still trading. THE TRADING-STATE COLUMN: `active` is this being null (Store.trading).

why a store stopped trading, where the source said: blank for a trading store, 'Closed' or 'Restructured' for an ended one, null on the online placeholder. Prose from the source, not a closed vocabulary of this bundle's own (rule Store.trading).
the store's floor area in square metres.
true on the online outlet (its site code is -1), false on every physical shop, never empty. Rule Store.channel reads `physical` as false and `online` as true.
true where the store closed for good (`status_annotation` is Closed), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Store.trading reads its `shut` option from it.
true where the store closed and was replaced (`status_annotation` is Restructured), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Store.trading reads its `restructured` option from it.

concepts.means:

WHICH CHANNEL THE SALE WAS IN — `physical` for a shop you can walk into, `online` for the web shop. Derived on the fact from the store key (`store_key = 999999` is the web shop), so it needs no join and is reachable from every question whatever route it takes. A FINANCIAL QUESTION THAT NAMES NO CHANNEL COVERS BOTH, by the operator's ruling of 2026-10-18 (rule Store.channel). Before this column that reading was the ABSENCE of a predicate, which no gate could check and no answer could disclose; now it can be grouped, stated and verified.

true on every web-shop line, false on every shop line, never empty; the same split as `channel`, as true / false. Made by the transform so that rule Order.channel reads its `shops` and `online` options from a column instead of a stored value.

THE COUNTRY OF THE SALE — the ISO code of the country this line is trade IN. A shop sale is attributed to the country the SHOP stands in; a web sale to the country the CUSTOMER lives in. Derived on the fact from `channel` and the two keys, so it needs no join and is reachable from every question whatever route the question takes. This is the reading an unqualified country question means (operator ruling 2026-10-25); the store's, the customer's and the site's own country stay askable BY NAME through their own relations. EVERY LINE REACHES A COUNTRY and none carries the `--` sentinel: the sentinel leaves the country axis of a sale entirely, because a web sale is attributed to a person and a person has a real country. The axis PARTITIONS the sales line — the parts sum to the whole, with no leakage and nothing double counted. The figures that prove it are in the ruling, which is their one home; a figure restated here would be a second home that goes stale on the next load. WHY IT IS NOT `dim_customer.country_code` UNDER ANOTHER NAME, though it is row-for-row identical to it here: no physical sale in this warehouse crosses a border, so the two readings AGREE BY ACCIDENT OF THE DATA. They do not mean the same thing — a German tourist buying in Paris is French trade on this column and German trade on the customer's — and the operator refused `default: customer` on 2026-10-22 for exactly that reason.

THE CURRENCY THE SALE WAS TRANSACTED IN, and NOT the unit of the amounts on this row. The amounts are USD. Filtering on this and presenting the amounts as if they were in that currency is forbidden by currency.ambiguity.code_is_not_the_unit_of_the_amounts.

THE CURRENCY THE AMOUNTS ON THIS ROW ARE IN — USD on every line, made by the transform. The upstream publishes it and the warehouse confirms it: the source's own exchange rate on each line is the USD-to-line-currency rate. It is the source currency the exchange-rate edge joins on (order__converts_at__exchange_rate), so the join reads a column instead of a constant. Offered to no question on its own; `currency_code` is the currency a sale was transacted in.
how many units of the product the line sold.

the price actually paid for one unit, in USD, after discount. Upstream: `unit_price * (1 - discount/100)`, and measured never above `unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: the price holds for every unit on the line, so it averages as Σ(quantity × net_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `net_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_is_per_article), never as a plain mean of line prices. The generator draws a quantity per order row and prices the row per unit (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").

what ONE UNIT ON THIS LINE was charged before discount, in USD. Measured against the source: `unit_price = product.Price × f`, where `f` is the same per-line factor used for `unit_cost = product.Cost × f`. From 2024 onward `f = 1.0`, so this is the current list price level for all products sold in that period. `gross_amount` is exactly `quantity * unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: Σ(quantity × unit_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `gross_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line prices (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").

what one unit cost Contoso, in USD. Upstream it is scaled by the same price factor as `unit_price`, so margin PERCENT is stable within a category while absolute margin moves — a margin-erosion story read off this data is an artefact of the generator. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`; Σ(quantity × unit_cost) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `cost_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line costs (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").

what the customer was actually charged for the line, in USD, after discount: exactly `quantity * net_price`. THE DEFAULT MONEY COLUMN: a question saying revenue or sales without saying net or gross is answered here (rule Order.revenue_means_net). AN UNQUALIFIED PRICE means what the customer paid per article: this column summed and divided by `quantity` summed (operator ruling, 2026-09-30; rule Order.price_is_per_article). When a question says store, shop, product, or placed without naming a competing figure, those words are read on this same sales-line figure.
what the line would have cost at list price, in USD: exactly `quantity * unit_price`, on every line. The figure BEFORE discount.
what the goods on the line cost Contoso, in USD. Measured: exactly `quantity * unit_cost`.
the money given away on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `gross_amount - net_amount`. Upstream the discount is an integer percent from a closed set of 15 steps, 0 to 14.
the profit on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `net_amount - cost_amount`, so it is margin on the DISCOUNTED price and not on list.

edges.means: Every customer carries a real country code and none carries the placeholder `--`, which marks the online channel. PARENT OPTIONAL, hence `0..N` and not `1..N`: a country with no customer exists, and check_edge_claims_proved refused the stronger claim (2026-09-30).
Two edges to Currency because the pair is ORDERED and inverting it is wrong by the rate squared.

Every location carries a country code and every code has a location, mandatory both ways. Location keeps its own `country_name` column, which is the SAME fact one hop closer; the name's home is Country.

THE PREDICATE IS DECLARED, AND THE `1` IS MEASURED — operator-approved 2026-10-08. A rate is picked by the order's day, the sale's currency as the target, and the currency the amounts are in as the source: that triple returns exactly one rate per sales line, which is what `cardinality: '1'` asserts; on the currency alone the join fans out to one rate per quoted day. The source side is the column `unit_currency` (USD on every line, made by the transform), not a constant written into this join, because an edge joins on columns (grammar v3). The source currency is the amounts' declared unit (`net_amount.offers.aggregate.unit`), confirmed in acceptance/verification/manual_value_check_2026-10-08.md — the sale's `currency_code` is the currency transacted in, not the unit of the figure. This edge converts USD amounts OUT to a local currency on request; it is never the way to "get USD". The business rule is Order.rate_on_order_date.
Every location has at least one store row and every store row stands at a location, mandatory both ways.
Every store row carries a country code and every code has a store, mandatory both ways — the store table is where the country set comes from, the online row's `--` included.

rules.says: A brand is the name a customer buys a product under; a manufacturer is who made it. The two sets overlap in names but are two notions, and a question asking who is behind a product says which it means rather than treating them as interchangeable.
A colour is one member however the source spells its case: colour names are capitalised, so Blue and blue are one colour. A breakdown or count by colour never lists two spellings of one colour.

The placeholder country code `--` is not a country. It marks rows that carry no real country, such as the online store. Questions about countries count and list real countries only, unless they name the placeholder.

A question asking for the countries where we have customers asks for countries: the countries at least one customer lives in, one answer row per country, never one row per customer. Country is the subject and Customer the restriction. The same reading holds for other existence phrasings — countries that have a customer, with any customer — and the question must be answered, not refused.

When a question asks for figures by country without saying whose country, a sale is attributed to the country it was made in: a shop sale to the country the shop stands in, an online sale to the country the customer lives in. Every sale reaches exactly one country, so the parts add up to the whole. A question may instead ask by store country, customer country or site country and gets that reading. The answer says which country it used.

Every amount on a sale is in US dollars. A sale's currency is the currency the customer transacted in, not the unit of its amounts: filtering by that currency does not turn the amounts into it. Sales asked for in a named currency are converted through the exchange rate.

A currency is reached by three routes: the currency a sale was paid in, or one of the two currencies of an exchange rate — its source (the currency it converts from; for a sale, the currency the amounts are stored in) or its target (the currency it converts to; for a sale, the sale's own currency). A question that reaches a currency without saying which — from a sale, a store, a site or an exchange rate — is answered on the currency the sale was paid in; a question may name the rate's source or target currency instead. The answer says which currency it used.

A customer is active on a reference date when that date falls inside the customer's validity window — on or after the day the record became valid and on or before the day it stopped being valid. The reference date is the date the question states, else the data's own "now", and the answer says which. "Customers" with no other word means the active customers; "registered" customers are every customer on the register, whether valid on that date or not. Active customers are not the same set as customers who have bought something — each can hold people the other does not.

An age is computed, never stored: a customer's age from the birth date and a store's age from its opening date, both measured at the sampling date rather than at today's date. Which age arithmetic is meant — completed years counting the birthday, or calendar year boundaries crossed — has not been ruled.

The customer register keeps history: a row is a version of a person, valid over a window. The customer as they are now and the customer a past sale was made to can be different rows, and reading one as the other moves old sales to new addresses. A question joining customers to sales over a period says which it means; neither reading is declared the default.

A figure "per customer" divides by a count of customers, and which customers it counts is a choice. By default it counts the buyers: the distinct customers on the sales lines the figure is summed over, so revenue per customer by country divides each country's revenue by the customers who bought in that country. The other options count the customers active on the reference date, or every customer on the register. The answer says which customers it divided by.

The customer register is wider than the buyers: a customer is a person on the register, and many registered customers have never bought anything. This is by design of the source, not a defect. "Customers" and "buyers" are two populations, and an answer counting customers says which one it counted.

An amount is converted at its own day's rate, never at a rate averaged over a period. A rate is not a quantity to add up: over time it can at most be averaged, and across currency pairs it is not combined at all.

An exchange rate's target currency means something only together with its source currency: the direction is part of the rate's identity, so a rate is never picked or grouped by its target currency alone.
The online store is recorded as a location, but it is not a place. Questions about locations and places cover physical locations only, unless they name the online channel.

A site counts as closed when a store at it has closed, whether or not another store trades there now. A question may ask instead for the sites where no store trades now. The answer says which it counted.

Site and location name the same notion: the place a store stands on, described by its country and its state or region. A store's place has no city in this business's data — its finest geography is the state or region — and a city is only where a customer lives, so a question about the cities stores are in has no answer here and must say so rather than offer site codes.

A sale is made in one of two channels: a shop you can walk into or the web shop. A figure of the sale that names no channel covers both channels, even when the question reaches the sale through stores; a question that names the shops or the web shop gets that channel. The answer says which channels it covered.
Cost means only what the goods cost Contoso to buy — the procurement cost. Every other money figure on a sale, gross, net, discount and margin, is revenue or income, never a cost.

An order's date is the day it was placed, not the day it was delivered. A question that says when, or names a period, without saying delivery is answered on the order date; a question that says delivered or shipped is answered on the delivery date.
A question about Order that names no figure reads `net_amount`; the other figures are read when named.
A discount percentage is the money given away divided by the gross amount before discount — not by the net amount.

A total discount is money: the sum of what was given away below the regular price on every discounted sale in scope. It is never a sum or an average of discount rates. The rate is meant only when the question names it — discount percentage, discount rate, average discount.

How many is three questions. Purchases are counted as orders; items sold are the quantity summed; order lines are how the data is stored and are not a business quantity. "How many did we sell" asks for items, "how many times did we sell" or "how many orders" asks for purchases.

An order is the purchase: one customer buying at one store on one day in one currency. Its lines are not orders and not events of their own — a line borrows the when, the who and the where from its order and adds only which product and how many. Counting orders counts purchases, never lines.
A margin ratio can be stated two ways over the same profit, and the question must say which: margin percent is profit over net revenue, markup is profit over cost. A question naming neither is asked.

An order has no state beyond its two dates: it was placed on one day and delivered on another. Nothing records a cancellation or a return, so a question about either has no answer in this business's data and says so; an absent state is never read as zero.

"Now", for this data, is the date of the newest order — measured from the data, not taken from the clock. Relative periods such as "last month" are read against it, and it moves forward by itself when new orders arrive.
A question that names no period covers all time. There is no implied "this year" and no implied latest month, and the answer states the window it covered.
An unqualified price means what the customer paid per article: the net amount divided by the number of units, both summed over the lines asked about — never an average of line prices.

Four facts on a sale carry every price and cost. The unit price is the regular, list price of one unit before discount; the net price is the actual selling price of one unit after discount; the unit cost is what one unit cost Contoso; the quantity is how many units. Every amount derives from them: gross is quantity times unit price, net is quantity times net price, cost is quantity times unit cost, discount is gross less net, and margin is net less cost — so margin is profit on the discounted price, not on list. "Unit price" names the regular price, not what was paid.
An amount is converted at the exchange rate of the order's own day. A rate is identified by its day and both of its currencies together; a target currency alone does not pick a rate.
"Revenue" or "sales" without "net" or "gross" means the net amount — what the customer was charged after discount — and the answer says so. "Gross revenue" means the amount before discount.

A product carries no standing price and no standing cost. A price changes over time, so every price and cost is the one on the sale, dated by the sale, and a product's price is reached through its sales. A product's current price is the regular unit price on its latest sale, stated with that sale's date where it matters. A question qualifying products by price — high-value products — selects products by that price and then counts all their sales, never qualifies individual sale lines.
A product category is the top level of the product hierarchy. A question saying category is answered on the category; one saying sub-category is answered on the sub-category.

A store is a shop you can walk into. The online channel is recorded as a store, but a question about stores — how many there are, which ones — covers physical shops only unless it names the online channel. That default holds only when the question is about stores: revenue and every other figure of the sale includes both channels, even when the question's route passes through stores.

A store is the premises Contoso sells from: a shop standing on one place for one trading period, with its own name, floor area, opening date and closing date. It is part of a location, not the location itself — one place may hold a succession of premises over time, each of them a store. So one store is counted and listed by its premises, and a count, list or sum over stores is a different question from the same figure over places; an answer that could be read at either level says which level it used. The site reading (one row per place, whatever premises it held) is the other option.

A question about what the store table records — how many store versions or rows there are, or a list of every restructured store — covers every recorded row, the online channel included, with no channel or trading-state restriction. "How many stores do we have" is a different question and keeps the physical and active defaults.

A store is active while it has no closing date. A store with a closing date is closed, and a closed store is either shut — closed for good — or restructured — closed and replaced. A question about stores covers active stores unless it names another state.
